entries.objective: Understand the seminar task and milestone expectations.
entries.prompt: Read the HW/SW Codesign seminar PDF and explain what must be delivered for the topic Force-Directed Scheduling for High-Level Synthesis.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI identified the seminar as a topic-based paper and presentation task, using the IEEE style, scientific writing, references, GitHub documentation, and an implementation-oriented elaboration.

actions: Checked the course PDF for paper length, presentation duration, IEEE template, plagiarism warning, GitHub usage, and elaboration items.
Compared the AI summary with the professor slide that lists mathematical basics, formal algorithm, runtime/overhead, C/C++ implementation, application example, and RTL output.

entries.reflection: This interaction fixed the boundary of the work: the milestone is not only a general summary but must prepare a technical and implementable seminar topic.

entries.objective: Clarify the exact topic and avoid neighboring-topic confusion.
entries.prompt: My assigned topic is Force-Directed Scheduling for High-Level Synthesis. Explain how it differs from list scheduling, ILP-based scheduling, and force-directed list scheduling.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI separated pure force-directed scheduling from list scheduling, ILP scheduling, and hybrid force-directed list scheduling, emphasizing that FDS is a heuristic for distributing operations across control steps to balance resource usage.

actions: Checked the possible-topic slide: Force-Directed Scheduling and Force-Directed List-Scheduling appear as separate topics.
Checked de Micheli contents: list scheduling, ILP, and force-directed scheduling are separate subsections under scheduling with resource constraints.

entries.reflection: The interaction prevented mixing multiple seminar topics and helped keep the paper focused on the assigned algorithm.

entries.objective: Build an initial technical vocabulary for HLS scheduling.
entries.prompt: Explain HLS, scheduling, allocation, binding, latency, control step, resource constraint, data-flow graph, ASAP, ALAP, mobility, and force in simple words but technically correct.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI produced a glossary connecting behavior-level descriptions to RTL datapath/control generation and positioned scheduling as the time-assignment step before binding.

actions: Compared the terminology with Teich/Haubelt sections on synthesis, scheduling, allocation, and binding.
Checked de Micheli contents for architectural synthesis, scheduling, resource sharing, and binding.

issues: Some explanations were simplified and had to be rewritten in stricter scientific language.

entries.reflection: The glossary was useful for learning, but final wording needed manual correction to avoid sounding like lecture notes.

entries.objective: Identify the main reference chapters.
entries.prompt: From de Micheli and Teich/Haubelt, which chapters are most relevant for Force-Directed Scheduling in HLS?
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI pointed to architectural synthesis, scheduling algorithms, scheduling with resource constraints, ASAP/ALAP scheduling, list scheduling, force-directed scheduling, and binding/resource sharing as the relevant reading area.

actions: Verified against de Micheli table of contents: Architectural Synthesis and Scheduling Algorithms include ASAP, ALAP, ILP, List Scheduling, and Force-directed Scheduling.
Verified against Teich/Haubelt table of contents: Ablaufplanung includes ASAP, ALAP, list scheduling, force-directed scheduling, and ILP.

entries.reflection: The interaction made the reading plan more efficient and avoided using unrelated chapters as main evidence.

entries.objective: Create a first research framing for the seminar paper.
entries.prompt: Give me a research framing for Force-Directed Scheduling for HLS: motivation, problem, algorithm idea, implementation target, and evaluation criteria.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI framed FDS as an architectural-synthesis heuristic that schedules operations from a CDFG under a latency bound while reducing peak functional-unit demand through a force metric.

actions: Checked that HLS output should lead to RTL components, matching the professor slide.
Validated that scheduling is the temporal-domain architectural synthesis problem in de Micheli.

issues: The first output overclaimed optimality; it was corrected to say heuristic, not exact optimum.

entries.reflection: This interaction shaped the scientific purpose: explaining why a heuristic is needed between simple lists and exact ILP.

entries.objective: Derive possible research questions.
entries.prompt: Formulate 3 to 5 research questions for a seminar paper on Force-Directed Scheduling for High-Level Synthesis.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI proposed questions about how FDS models operation mobility, how force balances resource usage, how it compares to ASAP/ALAP/list scheduling, and how a small implementation can demonstrate the main feature.

actions: Removed questions that were too broad for a five-page paper.
Checked whether each question can be answered with the main references and a small implementation.

issues: Some proposed questions involved modern commercial HLS tools, which were outside the milestone scope.

entries.reflection: The research questions became more realistic after limiting them to the professor-required elements.

entries.objective: Plan the M1 milestone structure.
entries.prompt: Create a professional Milestone 1 structure for technical understanding and research framing for this topic.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI suggested sections for scope, motivation, core terminology, main references, algorithm intuition, expected implementation, risks, and next steps.

actions: Compared the structure with the professor elaboration list.
Ensured the structure supports later milestones instead of becoming a final paper too early.

entries.reflection: This became the working outline for documenting M1 clearly.

entries.objective: Explain the role of CDFG/DFG in the topic.
entries.prompt: Why does Force-Directed Scheduling need a data-flow graph or sequencing graph? Explain for HLS.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI explained that operations become nodes and dependencies become directed edges; scheduling must assign each operation to a legal control step while respecting predecessor-successor constraints.

actions: Checked Teich/Haubelt modeling section on data-flow graphs and CDFGs.
Checked de Micheli contents for data-flow and sequencing graphs.

entries.reflection: This clarified that FDS is not scheduling CPU tasks but operation nodes inside a hardware behavior.

entries.objective: Understand ASAP and ALAP as support machinery.
entries.prompt: Explain ASAP and ALAP scheduling and why they are needed before force-directed scheduling.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI described ASAP as earliest legal time, ALAP as latest legal time under the latency bound, and mobility as the allowed range in which FDS evaluates candidate assignments.

actions: Checked de Micheli scheduling subsections for ASAP and ALAP.
Manually tested the idea on a small dependency chain.

entries.reflection: This interaction established the foundation for the later mathematical description.

entries.objective: Understand the meaning of force intuitively.
entries.prompt: Explain force in force-directed scheduling as if I am new to the topic, then restate it technically.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI explained force as the change in resource-demand distribution caused by fixing an operation to a specific step; technically, it relates candidate placement to operation probability and resource usage over the operation time frame.

actions: Checked against the known FDS idea: distribution graph and force computation are the central mechanism.
Marked the intuitive explanation as learning support, not as direct paper text.

issues: The analogy was useful but too informal for the submitted report.

entries.reflection: This made the core idea memorable but also showed that final writing must be more formal.

entries.objective: Choose a small application example for the paper.
entries.prompt: Suggest a small HLS scheduling example suitable for explaining FDS in a five-page seminar paper.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI suggested using a compact arithmetic data-flow graph with multiplications and additions so ASAP peak usage can be contrasted with force-directed spreading.

actions: Checked that the example is small enough to calculate manually.
Later aligned the example with the C++ implementation requirement and professor feedback.

issues: The first candidate graph had too many operations; it was reduced to a small five-operation example.

entries.reflection: The example choice became important because it connects explanation, implementation, and screenshots.

entries.objective: Create a reference-management plan.
entries.prompt: Give me a Zotero/Citavi note plan for sources related to Force-Directed Scheduling for HLS.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI proposed reference notes for de Micheli, Teich/Haubelt, the original force-directed scheduling paper, and supporting HLS overview references.

actions: Checked the course slide requiring reference-management notes.
Removed sources not directly used in the milestone.

issues: Some suggested citations needed manual bibliographic verification before use.

entries.reflection: This helped document not only citations but why each source matters.

entries.objective: Critique an overly general AI summary.
entries.prompt: Here is a general AI summary of HLS scheduling. Tell me what is missing for my specific topic FDS.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI identified missing details: ASAP/ALAP mobility, distribution graphs, self/predecessor/successor forces, candidate-step scoring, and a concrete implementation of the force function.

actions: Compared missing items with the professor elaboration list.
Confirmed that the missing items are essential to the algorithm, not optional additions.

entries.reflection: This interaction corrected the direction from general HLS to the specific FDS main feature.

entries.objective: Define scope exclusions.
entries.prompt: What should I not include deeply in a short Force-Directed Scheduling paper?
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI recommended not going deep into RTL synthesis, commercial HLS tools, full binding algorithms, advanced pipelining, and unrelated metaheuristics, except as brief context.

actions: Checked the page limit and required elaboration topics.
Kept implementation and application example inside the scope.

entries.reflection: The paper scope became manageable and less likely to lose focus.

entries.objective: Build an initial comparison table.
entries.prompt: Make a concise comparison of ASAP, ALAP, list scheduling, ILP scheduling, and FDS for HLS.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI drafted a table comparing purpose, optimality, complexity, resource awareness, and paper relevance.

actions: Checked de Micheli contents showing these algorithms as neighboring scheduling methods.
Rewrote wording to avoid unsupported claims about exact complexity.

issues: The first version said ILP is always impractical; this was softened to problem-size dependent.

entries.reflection: The table became a useful way to explain where FDS sits among other algorithms.

entries.objective: Validate the professor-specific deliverables.
entries.prompt: Match my topic work against the professor slide: math basics, formal description, algorithm, runtime, C/C++ implementation, application example, RTL output.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI created a checklist and mapped each required item to planned sections and future milestones.

actions: Checked the HW/SW Codesign PDF elaboration slide.
Marked C/C++ and RTL output as not optional for the final work.

entries.reflection: This made the milestone plan assessment-ready.

entries.objective: Translate learning explanation into scientific wording.
entries.prompt: Convert my simple Bangla/English learning notes about FDS into scientific English bullet points without copying textbook text.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI rewrote informal understanding into formal statements about behavioral synthesis, operation scheduling, latency constraints, and resource-demand balancing.

actions: Manually rewrote the output again to keep original authorship.
Checked terminology against source vocabulary.

issues: Direct text reuse was avoided because the professor emphasized intellectual origin.

entries.reflection: The interaction improved tone but reinforced the need for manual authorship.

entries.objective: Identify risks of AI hallucination.
entries.prompt: List likely AI mistakes when explaining force-directed scheduling and how I should validate them.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI listed risks such as confusing FDS with force-directed graph drawing, claiming global optimality, ignoring predecessor/successor forces, and misrepresenting RTL output.

actions: Checked each risk against the main references and course requirements.
Used this list as a validation checklist for later prompts.

entries.reflection: This interaction directly improved the reliability of later AI-assisted work.

entries.objective: Create a seminar-story explanation for personal understanding.
entries.prompt: Explain FDS like a story so I can remember it during discussion, then give the technical version.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI used a resource-balancing story and then restated the algorithm in terms of operations, time frames, distribution graphs, candidate assignment, and force minimization.

actions: Kept the story for oral understanding only.
Only the technical restatement influenced the written milestone.

issues: Story format is not suitable for the paper itself.

entries.reflection: The story helped retention, but it was not used as submitted text.

entries.objective: Prepare possible professor questions.
entries.prompt: What questions might the professor ask in M1 about FDS and how should I answer briefly?
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI prepared possible questions about why FDS is used, what force means, why ASAP/ALAP are needed, and what the implementation will demonstrate.

actions: Checked answers for consistency with the main scope.
Removed unsupported claims about industrial performance.

entries.reflection: This helped turn the milestone from a written summary into an explainable topic.

entries.objective: Evaluate whether the topic is implementation-feasible.
entries.prompt: Can I implement the main feature of Force-Directed Scheduling in C++ for a small example? What exactly should be implemented?
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI concluded that the main feasible feature is the force computation and candidate-step selection using ASAP/ALAP ranges, probabilities, and distribution graphs, not a complete industrial HLS system.

actions: Checked the professor slide requiring C/C++ implementation of the main feature.
Verified that a small DFG example can produce demonstrable output.

entries.reflection: This set the direction for M3 implementation and avoided overbuilding.

entries.objective: Summarize M1 decisions.
entries.prompt: Summarize the final M1 decisions for my Force-Directed Scheduling seminar topic.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI summarized the topic scope, references, terminology, research questions, planned example, implementation goal, and validation strategy.

actions: Compared the summary against all previous M1 notes.
Manually removed repeated and informal statements.

entries.reflection: M1 ended with a clear research frame and preparation path for M2.
